title: The RAD Float Trap: Why a Full Residential Aged Care Facility Can Still Run Short on Cash
linkedin:
A residential aged care facility can be at full occupancy, with a waitlist behind it, and still hit a genuine cash squeeze next month.

The reason rarely shows up in the trading figures. It sits inside the RAD pool.

A Refundable Accommodation Deposit is not revenue. It is a lump sum a resident pays for their room, which the facility must eventually repay when they leave. That obligation does not wait for convenient timing. Once a resident departs, the facility owes that deposit back within a fixed period, regardless of whether a new resident has moved into the room.

The pattern that catches operators out is a handful of long-stay residents, often the ones who arrived with the largest deposits years ago, leaving within a short window of each other. A single RAD refund can be a substantial outflow on its own. Several landing in the same quarter can outweigh a full quarter of operating surplus, even while every bed stays filled.

A new resident moving into the vacated room does not solve the timing problem either. Their deposit, if they pay one at all, arrives on its own schedule, often months later, and for a different amount.

The fix is not complicated. It means treating the RAD pool as its own forecasting line, separate from operating trading, built out far enough to see refund obligations coming before they land in the account balance.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog. Link in the first comment.

A note for residential aged care operators across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria.

It's a pattern we see often: a facility with every bed filled and a waitlist behind it can still face a genuine cash shortfall the following month. The reason usually is not the trading figures, it is the pool of Refundable Accommodation Deposits sitting behind the front door.

A RAD is not revenue. It is a lump sum a resident pays for their room, and the facility is required to hand it back once they leave, on a fixed timeline that does not wait for a convenient month. A handful of long-stay residents departing within a short window of each other can move more cash out than a full quarter of steady operating trading brings in, even while every bed stays filled the entire time.

The fix is straightforward once it is named: treat the RAD pool as its own forecasting line, separate from day-to-day operating income, built out far enough to see refund obligations coming.
